title: Framing a Machine Learning Problem
abstract:
Stage 1 of the MLDLC, treated in full. Seven questions turn a sentence a
stakeholder said into a specification an engineer can build against: business
problem to ML problem, type of problem, current solution, getting data, metrics
to measure, online versus batch, and check assumptions. This document works each
one, then applies all seven end-to-end to the Netflix churn example, and closes
with the traps — target leakage, an unactionable prediction, an unmeasurable
target, and a horizon nobody specified.

blocks.t: The Seven Questions

blocks.cap:
The framing sequence from the notes. Each step narrows the problem
 until it is buildable. Skipping any of them produces a project that runs for
 months before anyone notices it cannot succeed.

blocks.t: Why this stage has no code

The output of framing is a document, not a model. Its purpose is to make
the project falsifiable: if you cannot state what success looks like before you
start, you cannot recognise failure afterwards, and the project will simply
continue.

blocks.cap:
The same project before and after framing. Everything on the right is
 a decision somebody had to make; none of it comes out of the data.

blocks.t: Question 1 — Business Problem to ML Problem

The stakeholder describes an outcome they want. You must convert it into a
prediction with a subject, a horizon, and an action attached.

head: Business statement
ML statement
rows: For each active subscriber, predict $P(\text{cancels within 30 days})$ from behaviour up to today
For each SKU–store pair, predict units sold next week
For each transaction, predict $P(\text{fraudulent})$ before authorisation
For each incoming ticket, predict its category and priority

blocks.t: Two things that must be nailed down here

The target definition. "Churn" is not computable. "Cancelled the
subscription within 30 days of the snapshot date" is. Different definitions
produce different datasets, different base rates and different models — and
stakeholders often disagree with each other about which one they meant.

The prediction horizon. "Will churn" is not a prediction until you say
when. One day ahead is easy and useless — nothing can be done in a day.
Thirty days ahead is harder and actionable. The horizon must match the
time the business needs to act.
The actionability test

Ask: "when the model outputs 0.83, what does somebody do differently?"
If nobody can answer, stop — a prediction that changes no decision has no value
however accurate it is. Conversely, if the answer is "we call the customer",
then you have also learned that the model's job is to rank customers by
risk, not to classify them, because the call-centre capacity is fixed.
Question 2 — Type of Problem
Using the taxonomy from Topic 02:

rows: Is the target a number or a category?
Do we need an ordering rather than a label?
Does temporal order matter for splitting and features?

blocks.t: The framing choice is a real design decision

Churn can legitimately be posed three ways — binary classification (will they
churn?), survival analysis (how long until they churn?), or ranking (order
customers by risk). Each has a different loss, different metrics and a different
deployment. Choose deliberately, and record why.
Question 3 — Current Solution

What happens today? There is always something: a business rule, an
analyst's spreadsheet, a heuristic, or nothing at all.
This is your baseline and it defines the bar

If the current rule is "flag anyone inactive for 14 days" and it achieves
recall 0.31, then your model's job is to beat 0.31 — not to beat zero. Many
projects that report "85% accuracy" are quietly worse than the rule they
replaced. Measure the incumbent first, and write the number down.

Studying the current solution also tells you which features matter. If the
fraud team manually checks "distance from the previous transaction", that is a
feature you should build.
Question 4 — Getting Data

Does the data exist, who owns it, how far back does it go, and can you legally
use it? Topic 10 covers the sources. Three questions decide feasibility:

items:
Does the label exist historically? You cannot train a churn model
 if nobody ever recorded cancellations.

Will the features be available at prediction time? This is the
 one people miss — see the leakage box below.

How long is the label delay? For credit default you may wait two
 years to learn the outcome. That fixes your retraining cadence and how
 recent your training data can be.

blocks.t: Target leakage — the most expensive framing mistake

A feature that will not exist at prediction time, or that encodes the answer, will
give you a spectacular validation score and a worthless model.

head: Leaky feature
Why it is leakage
rows: Only populated after the customer churned
Contains future months when predicting in March
Includes calls made after the snapshot date

blocks.t:
The rule: every feature must be computable using only information
available strictly before the prediction timestamp. Draw the timeline and mark
the cut-off explicitly.
Question 5 — Metrics to Measure
You need two metrics and the mapping between them.

head: ML metric
Business metric
rows: Retained revenue from the save-offer campaign
Fraud losses avoided minus false-alarm cost

blocks.t: Deriving the threshold from the cost matrix

Metrics are not arbitrary — they follow from costs. If a false negative costs
$C_{FN}$ and a false positive costs $C_{FP}$, the expected cost of predicting
positive at probability $p$ is $(1-p)C_{FP}$ and of predicting negative is
$p\,C_{FN}$. Acting is optimal when
p > \frac{C_{FP}}{C_{FP}+C_{FN}}.

For churn, a save-offer costs ₹$200$ and a lost customer costs
₹$3000$, giving a threshold of $200/3200=0.0625$ — far from the
default $0.5$. Framing produces the threshold; it is not a modelling
detail.
Question 6 — Online vs Batch

Topic 03 in full. The framing question is narrower: how fast does the world
change, and how fast must the model follow?

rows: Can we score overnight, or must we answer in 50 ms?
You cannot retrain faster than labels arrive

blocks.t:
Churn is batch: risk changes over weeks, the retention team works from a list,
and scoring nightly is ample. Fraud is real-time: the answer must arrive before
the transaction is authorised.
Question 7 — Check Assumptions

The step everybody skips. Take the framing back to the people who will use the
output and confirm it.

items:
"You will act on the top 5{,}000 — is your team's capacity actually
 5{,}000 a month?"
"This assumes a save-offer changes behaviour. Has that been tested?"

"This assumes past churn patterns predict future churn. Did anything
 change — a price rise, a competitor launch?"

"This assumes the outcome is observable. Do we know when someone
 churned, or only when they stopped paying?"

blocks.t: Prediction is not intervention

A churn model predicts who will leave. It does not tell you who can
be persuaded to stay — those are different populations. Some customers will
leave regardless; some would have stayed without the offer, so the offer is pure
cost. The correct framing for a retention campaign is uplift modelling:
predict the change in retention caused by the treatment, not the outcome
itself. Raising this in an interview signals real experience.
Worked Example: Netflix Churn, All Seven Questions

rows: For every active subscriber, on the 1st of each month, predict the probability they cancel within the next 30 days, using only behaviour up to that date.
Supervised, binary classification. Deployed as a ranking — the retention team works a fixed-size list.
Rule: "flag anyone who has not watched in 14 days". Recall 0.31, precision 0.09. This is the bar.
Viewing events, session logs, billing history, plan changes, support tickets, device mix. 3 years available. Label from the billing table. All features cut off at the snapshot date.
ML: recall in the top decile of predicted risk. Business: incremental retained revenue, measured by A/B test. Threshold derived from ₹$200$ offer vs ₹$3000$ lifetime value $\to 0.0625$.
Batch. Scored nightly, retrained monthly. Latency budget is hours.
Retention team capacity is 5{,}000 calls/month — confirmed. Save-offer efficacy previously measured at 12% — confirmed. Price rise last quarter may have shifted behaviour — flagged as a drift risk.

blocks.t: Code: Turning the Framing into Code

"""The framing document, expressed as executable constraints."""
import numpy as np, pandas as pd

# =====================================================================
# Q1 -- TARGET DEFINITION AND HORIZON, made explicit
# =====================================================================
SNAPSHOT_DATE      = pd.Timestamp("2026-03-01")
HORIZON_DAYS       = 30          # decided by how long retention needs to act
FEATURE_CUTOFF     = SNAPSHOT_DATE                      # nothing after this
LABEL_WINDOW_END   = SNAPSHOT_DATE + pd.Timedelta(days=HORIZON_DAYS)

def make_label(cancellations: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.Series:
    """churned = cancelled strictly inside the horizon window."""
    in_window = (cancellations.cancel_date >  SNAPSHOT_DATE) & \
                (cancellations.cancel_date <= LABEL_WINDOW_END)
    return in_window.astype(int)

# =====================================================================
# Q4 -- LEAKAGE GUARD: every feature must respect the cut-off
# =====================================================================
def build_features(events: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    past = events[events.ts < FEATURE_CUTOFF]        # <-- the whole guard
    assert past.ts.max() < FEATURE_CUTOFF, "feature leakage: future data used"
    return past.groupby("user_id").agg(
        sessions_30d   = ("ts", lambda s: (s > FEATURE_CUTOFF -
                                           pd.Timedelta("30D")).sum()),
        days_since_last= ("ts", lambda s: (FEATURE_CUTOFF - s.max()).days),
        total_minutes  = ("minutes", "sum"),
    )

BANNED = {"cancellation_reason", "account_status", "churn_flag",
          "refund_issued", "total_spend_this_year"}

def assert_no_leaky_columns(df: pd.DataFrame) -> None:
    leaked = BANNED & set(df.columns)
    assert not leaked, f"target leakage: {leaked}"

# =====================================================================
# Q3 -- THE BASELINE. Measure the incumbent BEFORE modelling.
# =====================================================================
from sklearn.metrics import recall_score, precision_score

def current_business_rule(feats: pd.DataFrame) -> np.ndarray:
    return (feats.days_since_last > 14).astype(int).values

def report_baseline(feats, y):
    p = current_business_rule(feats)
    print(f"BASELINE  recall {recall_score(y, p):.3f}  "
          f"precision {precision_score(y, p, zero_division=0):.3f}")
    return recall_score(y, p)          # the number your model must beat

# =====================================================================
# Q5 -- THE THRESHOLD COMES FROM COSTS, NOT FROM 0.5
# =====================================================================
COST_FALSE_POSITIVE = 200      # rupees: a save-offer sent to someone who'd stay
COST_FALSE_NEGATIVE = 3000     # rupees: lifetime value of a customer lost

OPTIMAL_THRESHOLD = COST_FALSE_POSITIVE / (COST_FALSE_POSITIVE +
                                           COST_FALSE_NEGATIVE)
print("act when P(churn) >", round(OPTIMAL_THRESHOLD, 4))     # 0.0625

def expected_cost(y_true, prob, threshold):
    pred = (prob >= threshold).astype(int)
    fp = ((pred == 1) & (y_true == 0)).sum()
    fn = ((pred == 0) & (y_true == 1)).sum()
    return fp * COST_FALSE_POSITIVE + fn * COST_FALSE_NEGATIVE

# =====================================================================
# Q7 -- CAPACITY IS A HARD CONSTRAINT, so the metric is top-k recall
# =====================================================================
RETENTION_TEAM_CAPACITY = 5_000        # confirmed with the team

def recall_at_k(y_true, prob, k=RETENTION_TEAM_CAPACITY):
    """The only offline metric that matches how the model will be used."""
    top = np.argsort(-prob)[:k]
    return y_true[top].sum() / y_true.sum()

# =====================================================================
# Q2/Q6 -- TIME-AWARE SPLIT. A random split leaks the future into the past.
# =====================================================================
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit

def temporal_split(df, date_col="snapshot", cutoff="2026-01-01"):
    """Train on the past, validate on the future -- as production will run."""
    train = df[df[date_col] <  cutoff]
    test  = df[df[date_col] >= cutoff]
    return train, test
# Never use train_test_split(shuffle=True) on a temporal problem:
# it lets the model learn from March to predict January.

# =====================================================================
# THE FRAMING DOCUMENT AS A TESTABLE OBJECT
# =====================================================================
FRAMING = dict(
    business_problem = "subscribers are leaving",
    ml_problem       = "P(cancel within 30 days) per active subscriber",
    problem_type     = "supervised / binary classification / used as ranking",
    target           = "cancel_date in (snapshot, snapshot+30d]",
    horizon_days     = HORIZON_DAYS,
    baseline         = "inactive>14d rule, recall 0.31",
    ml_metric        = f"recall@{RETENTION_TEAM_CAPACITY}",
    business_metric  = "incremental retained revenue (A/B test)",
    threshold        = OPTIMAL_THRESHOLD,
    mode             = "batch: scored nightly, retrained monthly",
    action           = "top 5000 by risk receive a save-offer call",
    assumptions      = ["team capacity 5000/month",
                        "save-offer efficacy 12%",
                        "no structural change since the Q4 price rise"],
)
for k, v in FRAMING.items():
    print(f"{k:18s}: {v}")
Summary
Everything on one page

 target definition and a horizon.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked

Q. A stakeholder says "use ML to reduce churn". What are your first
three questions?

(1) How exactly do we define a churned customer, and over what horizon?
(2) What happens today, and how well does it work — what is the baseline?
(3) When the model flags someone, who does what, and how many can they handle?
The third question determines that the metric is recall@$k$, not accuracy.
Q. What is target leakage and how do you catch it?

A feature that encodes the answer or that will not exist at prediction time.
Catch it by drawing the timeline and enforcing a hard cut-off on every feature,
and by treating a suspiciously high validation score as a bug rather than a
success. Inspect the top features by importance — leakage almost always sits at
the top.
Q. Why not use 0.5 as the classification threshold?

Because 0.5 is only optimal when false positives and false negatives cost the
same, which is almost never true. The optimal threshold is
$C_{FP}/(C_{FP}+C_{FN})$. For churn, with a ₹$200$ offer and a
₹$3000$ customer, that is $0.0625$.

Q. Your churn model has AUC 0.89 but the retention campaign loses money.
Why?

Most likely you predicted the wrong quantity. The model ranks who will
leave; the campaign needs who can be persuaded to stay. Customers who
would have stayed anyway receive an offer at pure cost. The correct framing is
uplift modelling — estimate the treatment effect, not the outcome.
Q. How do you split data for a temporal problem?

Chronologically: train on the past, validate on the future, mirroring how the
model will actually run. A random shuffled split lets the model learn from March
to predict January, which inflates the score and cannot happen in production.
